exam: 1. A 35‑year‑old man presents with a tender swelling below the inguinal ligament that increases with coughing. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Femoral hernia; explain why the swelling is below the ligament and how to differentiate from an indirect inguinal hernia.

2. During a hernia repair you notice the inguinal ligament is thinner than usual. What could this indicate? — Possible previous surgery or chronic inflammation; discuss implications for incision placement.
3. A patient has a groin mass that is non‑reducible and the patient reports nausea. What urgent step should you take? — Suspect strangulation; arrange immediate surgical referral.

4. How does the inguinal ligament relate to the femoral triangle boundaries? — It forms the lower border; the triangle is bounded superiorly by the inguinal ligament, medially by sartorius, and laterally by adductor longus.
5. In a low‑resource setting, which bedside sign can help you confirm the presence of a femoral hernia? — A palpable, deep trough in the femoral triangle with a bulge below the ligament.
6. Why is an incision 2–4 cm above the inguinal ligament preferred for open hernia repair? — It avoids the femoral vessels and provides better access to the canal.
7. What is the clinical significance of the lacunar ligament in relation to the inguinal ligament? — It completes the medial floor of the femoral triangle and helps prevent femoral herniation.
8. A patient with a history of HIV presents with a groin mass. What differential should you consider? — Inguinal lymphadenopathy, tuberculosis, or a femoral hernia; discuss distinguishing features.
ai.title: Inguinal Ligament
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The inguinal ligament is a fibrous band from ASIS to pubic tubercle forming the floor of the femoral triangle and the upper border of the inguinal canal. It anchors key structures and guides hernia repair incisions.

sections.p: The inguinal ligament is the most superficial structure of the lower abdominal wall, running obliquely from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the pubic tubercle. It forms the lower border of the femoral triangle and the upper border of the inguinal canal.
It is a thickened inferior margin of the external oblique aponeurosis. The ligament is about 10–12 cm long, slightly convex, and attaches to the fascia lata at its lower end.
Superiorly it is covered by the external oblique muscle. Inferiorly it lies just above the femoral vein and artery. Medially it blends with the lacunar (Hesselbach) ligament.

t.b: Identify the ligament as the lower margin of the triangle; a shallow trough indicates normal thickness

sections.p: Arterial supply is from the inferior epigastric artery and branches of the femoral artery.
No major nerves run within the ligament; the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves lie superficial to it.
It provides a firm attachment for the abdominal wall, limits downward displacement of the femoral vessels, and serves as a landmark for surgical incisions.

b: Inguinal hernia repair incisions are made 2–4 cm above the ligament
sections.p: The ligament is a key landmark in inguinal hernia repair. Its integrity is essential for maintaining the femoral triangle’s shape.

t.b: A discontinuity may indicate a femoral hernia

sections.p: On the bedside, feel for a smooth, firm band from ASIS to pubic tubercle. In a femoral hernia, the ligament remains intact but the femoral triangle is widened.

t.b: A deep trough suggests the femoral vessels are displaced

whenToSeekHelp: Severe groin pain with swelling that rapidly enlarges, signs of strangulation (fever, vomiting, tachycardia)
